alt: The Criterion B specification feeds all four parts of criterion D: designing tests, carrying them out and judging each point, identifying improvements, and explaining the impact on the client or target audience. A vague specification leaves nothing precise to test against.
caption: Every test, judgement and improvement traces back to a specification point.

alt: Each specification point gets a method, a success measure taken from the specification, data to record, and who tests it where; for example, the sag test loads 2 kg three times against a 5 mm target. Below, test types run from quantitative (performance tests, questionnaires) through both (user trials, comparison tests) to qualitative (interviews, expert appraisal).
caption: Plan the test, the pass mark and the data before you test; use numbers and comments together.

after: ## Part 2: Carrying out tests and evaluating success
alt: Five specification points with target, result and judgement. Sag: mean 4.0 mm against 5 mm, met. Mass: 1.35 kg against 1.20 kg, 12.5% over, not met. Folding: 70% under 20 seconds against 80%, not met. Cost: £9.40 against £12, met. Carrying: 75% rated 4 or 5, met. The overall judgement links the two failures to the heavy hinge.
caption: Judge each point from the data, and report the failures honestly.

after: ## Part 2: Carrying out tests and evaluating success
alt: Dot plot of ten folding times from 13 to 25 seconds against a 20-second limit. The mean is 18.0 seconds, under the limit, but only 7 of the 10 players (70%) folded the stand in under 20 seconds, so the target of at least 80% is not met.
caption: Test what the specification actually asked for: here a proportion, not a mean.

alt: A weak improvement just says “make it lighter and easier to fold”. A strong one names the evidence, gives a specific change such as a lighter hinge or a larger thumb catch, explains why it would work, checks it does not undo the passed sag test, and plans a re-test.
caption: An improvement comes from a test result and ends with a plan to re-test.

after: ## Part 4: Explaining the impact on the client or target audience
alt: Five categories of impact for the music stand: use (faster set-up, fewer trips), wellbeing and ergonomics (lighter, but corners need rounding), cost and resources, environment (recyclable plywood, reusable hinge) and the wider community. A negative impact is included: the stand is too heavy for the youngest players.
caption: Impact is the difference the solution makes to people, good and bad, not a list of features.
